text: Find a practice from an unrelated field that has already solved a similar problem, and move it over to this one.
Take one premise that the question assumes to be true, reverse it, and see what becomes possible.
Stand fully in the place of the person most affected, and start from the moments that person actually meets in a day.
First list the resources that are already at hand but unused. Every idea must use at least one of them.
First write down the parts, roles or materials that the usual way is made of. Every idea replaces one of them with something else and says why it still works after the change.
Find two steps, objects or roles that are now kept apart. Every idea joins one such pair into one, so that the joining itself produces the effect.
First list the steps everyone believes cannot be left out. Every idea removes one of them completely, then finds a way for things to work without it.
Find things that already exist but were not made for this problem. Every idea moves one of them over and uses it here.
First write down the present order of events. Every idea changes the order in one place, or swaps who acts first and who acts second.
Assume only one tenth of the present time, money or people is left, so the usual way must fail. Start from that condition. The hard constraints still hold.

First pick a limit that the question does not state as a hard constraint but that everyone assumes. Assume it is gone, find a way, then change that way until it also works in reality. The hard constraints themselves cannot be lifted.
The goal is not a small gain but ten times better. First say why the usual way cannot reach ten times. Every idea must be a different path that can.
First break the problem into a few facts that cannot be broken down further. Cite no existing practice; build a way up from those facts alone.
First find a contradiction: making one thing better makes another worse. Every idea must make both hold at once, with no compromise.
Cut the subject into parts by time, place, group of people or situation. Every idea treats one part in a way that differs from the rest.
First list ways to make this problem worse, as concrete as you can. Then reverse each one to get an idea.
Pick any three concrete objects that have nothing to do with the question, such as a fishing net, a street lamp, a till receipt. Every idea must start from one property of one of them.
Assume the problem is given in turn to people of other trades, such as an emergency doctor, a game designer, a freight dispatcher. Every idea uses a habitual move from one such person's daily work.
